Okay, so I'm completely new to everything computer and everything programming. I've only been doing this for 1 month and 1 day and I've got down the basics of HTML, CSS and JavaScript. However, I'm stuck. I don't know where to go from here. Do I learn another language? Should I try to create something? Should I learn more about the logic of computers and programming in general? What?

Thanks.

Should I try to create something?

Of course, that's what programming is for. Go do something with your new skill. Write a tool to improve your life, make a game, find something interesting that's done with the tools you know and try to replicate it.

Should I learn more...

Always! As your next step I would suggest learning a tool set that allows you to make stand alone applications. Something like Processing might be a good start.

I agree: you should try to create something, anything, and in the road you will find things that you don't know how to do, you will google that and you will learn something new.   If you feel that you haven't learned enough and you want to practice, you can try for example: http://www.codewars.com/, there you will find hundreds of exercises in different languages and of different difficulty. After you complete each exercise, you can see the solutions of the rest of the users that have completed the same exercise and discuss about them. [Edit: I fixed the typo in the site URL]

I'll save the link. It appears they're currently trying to sell their domain.

Thanks for the help.

I think a good next step would be to learn about how HTTP works. The ins and outs of the protocol. This is something I skipped over early in my web dev career. I thought it didn't apply to me because I focused on front end development but that was short sighted of me. When I began to transition into more full stack web dev (which, lucky for you is easier these days for front end devs because of Node.js) there were knowledge gaps with regard to client-server architecture.

Definitely create something though as others have suggested. I am assuming you are interested in web development since you've taken the time to learn the CSS/HTML/JS trifecta, so a web page/app seems like the road you are headed down. Attempting to create a full blown app would be an invaluable learning experience AND it has the added benefit of being easily shown off to employers/clients, if that is your thing.

• Solve some Javascript katas
  • Browse GitHub and look for some projects you could contribute to
  • Start your own small project

I would say, do whatever peeks your interest and until then just stick with JavaScript. You can't learn a language in a month. There are far too many things to learn, especially about JS. If you feel that you have a good grasp of it, start learning about design patterns, closures and scope, as well as try to learn a good framework, do you know jQuery or just pure JS? Have you worked with Angular? Have you worked with callbacks and promises? Stepped into Node.JS at all? I mean there's a ton more.

Not trying to patronize you or question whether you learned it or not, it's just I don't necessarily think you should just jump off into trying to learn a new language quite yet. If you are learning how to program to get a job in the future you should look up some front-end dev interview questions and see if you can answer the majority of them. You probably already know this but there is always more to learn. I think if you wanted to take a little break from learning about JS then "the logic of computers and programming in general" would be a good place to go to. Although a lot of that stuff won't really help you much with JS specifically, it does help when it comes time to switch over to something else and will make it way easier to do so.

For HTML/CSS do basically the same thing I suggested for JS (try to expand your knowledge) and then look at responsive and adaptive web page design, design patterns (check out some boilerplates) and page speed optimization specifically, as well as maybe a little bit of SEO. There are so many people out there that know HTML/CSS/JS but don't know them well. So you end up with stuff like blocking scripts and huge files being loaded on mobile, pages not working/looking the same in different browses and OSes (fuck IE 7) and stuff not being responsive or adaptive. Again, not saying you shouldn't try other things, just saying there is a ton more to learn. Good luck!

Overestimating technological advances. There's plenty of blatant examples like Terminator, 12 Monkeys, or Back to the Future.

But my pet peeve example is Minority Report. Supposedly in 25 years Washington D.C.'s highways are completely overhauled to interact with ubiquitous hovercars. Overhauling infrastructure in a major urban area takes FOREVER. One reference point is NYC's 2nd Avenue subway line, which was originally proposed in 1929, although serious steps towards it really only started in 2005. The first phase is planned for completion beginning 2017 (and personally I don't think even that's likely). And that's without integrating radical new technologies. Another reference point is Elon Musk's hyperloop - he's said that he could build a hyperloop PROTOTYPE in 3-4 years, and I'm sure the actual thing would take at least 3x that long between politics, funding, safety testing, environmental impact, and all that other fun public transportation/infrastructure stuff. For making the magnet highway operational on the scale we saw in the movie, we'd likely have to have started planning it right around when the movie came out.
